scenes.text:
The crate rode high on Wren's back, roped to the frame at four points, and it had not shifted once in eleven miles. That was the trouble with a good load. A bad load told you where it was. A good one only got heavier.

The Ferrous Gate came up out of the haze the way it always did, all at once — two iron uprights sunk into the roadbed and a lintel between them with nothing above it, no wall, no fence, nothing to stop a man walking around. Men had tried walking around. The Road counted that as a debt too, and priced it worse.

Wren stopped at the white line eight paces short and let the frame's foot down onto the stone. His shoulders kept the shape of the straps.

The toll board hung on the left upright, and the System kept it current:

**FERROUS GATE — POSTED TOLL**
**Passage, laden: 7 days**
**Sealed cargo: subject to inspection**

Seven. He had walked this stretch expecting seven. He worked his thumb under the strap where it had cut in and watched the numbers, because sometimes they moved while you watched.

The collector's window was a slot in the right upright, elbow height, and Haro's ledger came out through it before Haro did — a great splayed book with a spine like a wagon axle, laid flat on the sill. Then the man. Long grey coat, gate-keys on a ring he never seemed to use, a face that had been reading columns for a long time.

"Name."

"You know my name."

"The book doesn't." Haro didn't look up. "Name."

"Idren." He said it the way he always said it, like a word from someone else's language. "Wren, on the road."

Haro's pen found the line. **IDREN — porter, indentured, Ferrous Gate.** Below it a column of small dates going back a year and a bit, each with a number beside it, and at the bottom two figures Wren had learned to find without reading the rest.

**Days owed: 4,027**
**Days paid: 52**

"Laden," Haro said. "Sealed?"

"Sealed."

"Set it down."

Wren backed the frame against the upright and unhooked the ropes, and the crate came off his spine with that awful lightness that is not relief. Pale wood, banded, and across the lid a wax seal the colour of a healed burn, pressed with a mark he did not know and had not asked about. He had carried it since the low bridges. It did not slosh. It did not knock. Whatever was in it fit exactly.

Haro came out through the gate's small door, walked around the crate once, and set two fingers on the seal without breaking it. He stood like that a moment, the way a physician stands.

"Seven for the passage," he said. "Two for the seal. Gate's discretion on unopened cargo."

"The board says seven."

"The board says *sealed cargo: subject to inspection.* This is the inspection." Haro took his fingers off the wax. "Nine days."

Wren did the arithmetic he had done a thousand times and would do a thousand more, and it came out the same as it always came out: no. Nine was nine. Nine was a fortnight of some winter forty years off, some afternoon he would now not have, spent here, standing on cold stone, arguing about wax.

"Nine," he said.

"Consent aloud. You know the form."

"I consent to the toll of nine days against passage of the Ferrous Gate, laden and sealed."

The System took them.

It was not pain. He had told a man once it was not pain and the man had not believed him, and Wren had stopped explaining after that. It was subtraction. Something in the meat of him that had been counting quietly since birth stepped back nine, and his knees knew it before he did, and the cold in the stone came up through his boots and found less to push against than it had a minute ago. He breathed out. The haze past the gate looked exactly as it had.

**TOLL PAID — 9 days**
**FERROUS GATE — passage granted, laden, sealed**

Haro was already writing. The pen went across the ledger in three motions, and Wren watched the two figures at the foot of the column get struck through and set again beneath.

**Days owed: 4,018**
**Days paid: 61**

Then the receipt: a chit of grey card, the day's mark pressed into it wet, pushed across the sill with one finger.

Wren took it. He got his own book out of his coat — a cheap thing, sewn, the first four pages swollen from a river — and he wrote the date and *Ferrous, laden+seal, 9* and the running total under it in his own hand, because a man who does not keep his own count is only borrowing somebody else's.

He was writing the 61 when he looked up the page.

Above his line, the last porter's: a woman's name he didn't know, four entries, and at the foot of them a paid-total that did not match what the four entries added to. Not by much. By one.

"Something," Haro said.

"No." Wren blew on the ink. "Nothing."

He shouldered the frame and took the crate's weight back onto a spine nine days shorter, and walked under the lintel, and the iron did not touch him.

The road between the gates ran chalk-white and slightly downhill, which was worse. Downhill made the crate want to walk ahead of him, and he spent four miles leaning back against a box that weighed nothing it hadn't weighed yesterday.

The Chalk Gate was a lesser post and looked it: one upright, no lintel, a slate board bolted to the stone and a shutter behind it. Somebody had swept the apron. That was the only sign anyone had been proud of the place in a long time.

**CHALK GATE — POSTED TOLL**
**Passage, laden: 5 days**
**Sealed cargo: subject to inspection**
**Query of account: 2 days**

He read the last line twice. It had not been on the Ferrous board. It might have been there all along on this one; he had come through the Chalk Gate empty a dozen times and never had cause to look past the second line.

The shutter went up. The collector was a broad woman in a coat too big for the weather, grey at the temples, a strip of leather round her wrist where a pen had worn her.

"Down," she said.

Wren set the frame's foot on the stone and let the straps go slack without taking them off. "Laden. Sealed."

"I can see both." She came out and around and looked at the crate the way a farrier looks at a hoof — from underneath, at an angle, without touching. Then she saw the wax and stopped looking casual about it.

The seal was the colour of a healed burn. The mark in it was the same mark it had been at the low bridges: three strokes and a closed loop, pressed clean.

"Who put this on."

"It was on when I took it."

"That's not an answer, porter."

"It's the one I've got."

She breathed out through her nose. She did not put her fingers on the wax the way Haro had. She stepped back from it, in fact, half a pace, and Wren noticed that and filed it beside the other things he was keeping.

"Five days," she said. "Passage."

"Nothing for the seal?"

"The seal isn't mine to price." She said it flat, the way a woman says a rule she has decided not to have feelings about. "Discretion on unopened cargo sits with the Ferrous window. You've already had it read there. I don't read it twice."

"He took two for it."

"Then he took two for it." She was already turning back to the sill. "Five, here. Consent aloud."

"I consent to the toll of five days against passage of the Chalk Gate, laden and sealed."

The System took them, and it was the same as it always was and never got any less strange: not pain, only a stepping-back. Some clock in the meat of him that had been counting since he was born went five smaller. His hands stayed steady. The chalk dust on his boots stayed chalk dust. Somewhere a long way ahead of him, an evening he had never seen went out like a lamp in a room he wasn't in.

**TOLL PAID — 5 days**
**CHALK GATE — passage granted, laden, sealed**

The book came out onto the sill. Same book. He had assumed, the first year, that every gate kept its own; it did not. It was one ledger and it went where it was needed, spine like a wagon axle, and his page was his page wherever it opened.

She found the line. **IDREN — porter, indentured, Ferrous Gate.** The column of small dates. Yesterday's entry in Haro's hand, the nine, the strike-through, the two figures set beneath.

She wrote today's. Her hand was rounder than Haro's and she pressed harder. Then she went to the foot of the column, struck the old totals, and set the new ones.

Wren read them upside down, which he had learned to do the way a man learns a road.

**Days owed: 4,021**
**Days paid: 66**

He did the sum before he could stop himself, and it was not a hard sum. Yesterday's owing had been four thousand and eighteen. He had just paid five. Four thousand and thirteen. He had been carrying that number since the lintel; he had walked eleven miles with it sitting behind his teeth.

Four thousand and twenty-one was not four thousand and thirteen. It was eight the wrong way. It was eight days of some spring he had not been introduced to, arriving on the page while he stood over it.

He looked at the paid column. Sixty-six was right. Sixty-one and five. She had added correctly there, in front of him, with the same pen, in the same minute.

Between the two figures, in the margin, there was a narrow ruled column he had never once had reason to look at, and in it, against today, a small letter and a numeral. He could not read the letter upside down. It might have been a C.

"Something," she said, not unkindly.

**Query of account: 2 days.**

Two days to ask. Two days to be told, probably, that the book was the book. Two days of some winter, spent on a question a woman who did not price seals would not be permitted to answer.

"No," Wren said. "Nothing."

She pushed the chit across. He took it, and got out his own cheap sewn book, and wrote the date, and *Chalk, laden, 5*, and under it, in his own hand, in his own count: **4,013.**

Then he underlined it, which he had never done before.

He shouldered the frame. The crate came up onto his spine, and it weighed what it had weighed at the low bridges, and he walked past the one upright into the white afternoon with two numbers in him now, going in different directions.

[STATUS] wren — Level 2 | HP 19/22 | MP ?/? | Gold ?

The paper liner was the discovery, and he made it sitting in a ditch outside the Chalk Gate with the crate on its side.

The seal was on the lid. Nobody had said anything about the bottom. Under the banding, where the pale wood met the base boards, somebody at the low bridges had tucked a sheet of packing paper up over the rim and creased it flat — a hand's width of it, dry, blank, folded in against the grain. He worked a finger under and drew out an inch and let it go back. It came out and went back without a sound.

He had a pencil stub. He wrote small, in a hand he'd taught himself the winter his ink froze: *Ferrous, 9, 61.* Under it: *Chalk, 5, 66.* Under that, his own running owed — *4,013* — and the book's, *4,021*, and between them a short stroke like a man drawing a line under a fight he intended to finish.

Then he pushed the paper back under the rim, and rolled the crate upright, and put his shoulder into the straps, and started the circuit.

The Slate Gate came at dusk of the second day, in that hour when a road holds the last of the light in its dust and nothing else does. One collector, a boy really, with a coat he'd grow into. No queue. No one behind Wren on the white for four miles; he had turned to check twice, and told himself both times that he was checking the weather.

"Laden. Sealed."

"Four days, laden." The boy did not look at the wax at all. "Consent aloud."

"I consent to the toll of four days against passage of the Slate Gate, laden and sealed."

The subtraction came and went. A stepping-back, some hour in a season with a name he'd never learn, gone quiet.

The book came out onto the sill, spine like an axle. Wren read upside down while the boy wrote, and he had his own numbers ready before the pen touched paper, because he always had them ready now.

**Days owed: 4,020**
**Days paid: 70**

Four thousand and twenty-one, less four, was four thousand and seventeen. The paid column was perfect. It was always perfect. And in the narrow ruled margin beside today the boy had set a small letter and a numeral without appearing to decide to, the way a man writes his own name.

Wren got out his sewn book. *Slate, laden, 4.* **4,009.**

Three the wrong way. Eight had become eleven, and he had watched it happen, and the boy had done nothing but write.

The Rushet Gate was two days on and there were people at it.

That was the whole of the difference and he did not know it yet. A grain wagon ahead, its driver arguing about axle-width. Two porters behind, one of them a big Sedge-country woman with a strapped-up knee who nodded at him the way porters nod, meaning *you're carrying that wrong and I'm not going to say so.* The collector worked with three of them watching and a fourth waiting.

"Six, laden," she said. "Consent."

"I consent to the toll of six days against passage of the Rushet Gate, laden and sealed."

Six went. He put a hand on the upright and took it off again before anyone could call it leaning.

The pen went across. The strike-through. The new figures.

**Days owed: 4,014**
**Days paid: 76**

He read it twice. Four thousand and twenty, less six. Four thousand and fourteen.

Correct. Correct to the day, in front of a grain driver and a woman with a bad knee.

The margin column beside today was empty.

He walked out from under nothing — Rushet had no lintel either — and got four hundred yards down the white before he stopped and stood there with the crate high on his spine and his heart going in a way that had nothing to do with the load.

The Millrace crossing was in the dark and in rain, alone, and cost three, and the book took four more than it should have and put a letter in the margin. He cut his hand getting the liner out of the crate rim with wet fingers, a long shallow tear across the heel of the thumb from the banding, and wrote the entry anyway with blood in the crease of the paper. He slept under the frame. He woke stiff and cold with the rain still going and something in his chest that rattled when he breathed out, and he got up and walked, because that was the arrangement.

The Sedge Gate had a road-warden standing at the sill on some business of his own, and cost five, and the book was flawless.

He sat down on the apron afterward, out past the post, and pulled the liner sheet out with his good hand and unfolded it across his knee.

Six entries. Six tolls. The paid column right every time — sixty-one, sixty-six, seventy, seventy-six, seventy-nine, eighty-four — a man's spent life added correctly at every single window on the Road.

And beside three of them, where he'd written *alone*, the owed number had climbed. Beside the three where he'd written *queue*, *driver + 2*, *warden*, it had not.

Fifteen days. Fifteen days of some spring, taken out of him in a margin.

He wrote *ALONE* across the top of the sheet in letters big enough to read at arm's length, and folded it, and pushed it back under the rim where a man would have to break the collector's own seal to get at it.

Then he stood up, slower than he meant to, and turned back toward the Ferrous Gate.

[STATUS] wren — Level 2 | HP 16/22 | MP ?/? | Gold ?

The relay before the Hask cut was a roof on four posts and a board, and the board had a new sheet nailed over the old one.

**THROUGH-CARRY — DOUBLE LADEN**
**Consignment to the Ferrous window, Ovenstone and Hask, no lay-over**
**Delivered by second dusk: CREDIT 3 DAYS AGAINST OWING**

Three days back. Not paid, not spent — back. He read it standing under the eave with the rain coming off it in a line behind his heels, and it was the first time in four years the Road had offered him a number that went the right way.

The Sedge-country woman was sitting against a post with her leg out straight and the strapping off her knee, and the knee looked like a thing that had been argued with and won.

"That's mine," she said, nodding at a plain crate roped in three places, no wax on it, nothing on it. "Was mine. I'm not walking it."

"How long have you got?"

"Second dusk. So, none." She looked at his frame, at the sealed crate already on it, and did the sum a porter does without meaning to. "You'd be double from here. Two gates, no sit-down. That's not a carry, that's a wager."

"It's three days."

"It's three days," she agreed, and she said it the way the Chalk collector had said *then he took two for it*. Then: "Nobody takes the through-carry twice. Ask around. Everyone's got a cousin who did it the once."

"Did the once and what?"

She shrugged with the shoulder that still worked. "Nobody says. That's what I'm telling you."

He roped her crate onto the top of his own, which meant the seal was buried, which he minded more than he expected to. The banding opened the tear across the heel of his thumb again while he pulled the last hitch. He wound a rag on it and got under the frame and stood up into a weight that was not twice what he'd been carrying but felt like more than twice, because the second crate sat high and wanted to steer him.

The Ovenstone gate was eleven miles on, and the schedule put him there at three in the morning, and he understood that before he'd gone a mile. That was the shape of the thing. Second dusk from here meant walking the hours when the road was empty. The bonus did not send you fast. It sent you alone.

He walked anyway.

The shoulder went at the eighth mile. Not a snap — a slow giving, up under the collarbone on the left, where the strap had been riding wrong since the second crate started steering. It let go in a long hot line and then would not take the load at all, and he had to stop in the middle of the white and shift everything onto the right, which put the whole double weight on one side of a man whose chest already rattled when he breathed out.

He stood there in the dark doing that arithmetic. Three days. Three days back, off four thousand and ten, on a page he'd stopped believing.

He went on, listing, at about the pace of a funeral.

The Ovenstone collector came out of the shutter buttoning his coat, alone, in a black hour with nothing on the road behind for as far as the dark went.

"Seven, double laden."

"I consent to the toll of seven days against passage of the Ovenstone Gate, laden double and sealed."

The stepping-back. Seven of them, all at once, which was a different feeling from five — some week he'd never be introduced to, folded away.

The book on the sill. He read upside down with his head at a bad angle because his left side would not come round.

**Days owed: 4,007**
**Days paid: 91**

Four thousand and ten, less seven, was four thousand and three. The paid column was perfect. In the narrow ruled margin, a small letter and a numeral, set down without a pause.

Four the wrong way.

Hask was six miles further and he did them in the grey, and the collector there was a thin man who wanted to be asleep and did not look at the wax at all, only at the plain crate and the consignment tag.

"Six, double."

"I consent to the toll of six days against passage of the Hask Gate, laden double and sealed."

Six went.

"Through-carry," Wren said, before the pen moved. "Ovenstone and Hask, no lay-over. Second dusk isn't until tonight."

"I can see the tag." The man wrote a while. Then he turned the book and did something Wren had never seen a collector do, which was set the pen down and use one finger to show him the line, right way up, like a favour.

**TOLL PAID — 6 days**
**THROUGH-CARRY COMPLETED — CREDIT 3 DAYS**
**Days owed: 4,003**
**Days paid: 97**

"There," the thin man said, almost kindly. "Not many get that."

Wren looked at the four figures for a long moment with his shoulder burning and his breath going in and out with a sound in it.

Four thousand and seven, less six, was four thousand and one. Less the three credited was three thousand nine hundred and ninety-eight. The book said four thousand and three.

He took the chit and got out past the post and sat down on the apron, badly, and worked the liner sheet out from under the crate rim with his right hand alone, and unfolded it on his knee under **ALONE**.

*Ovenstone, double, 7, alone.* *Hask, double, 6, alone.* *Credit, 3.*

His own running number at the foot: **3,979.** The book's: 4,003.

Fifteen had become twenty-four. They had given him three days with a line ruled under them and a man's finger pointing, and taken nine in a margin in the dark on the road they'd sent him down to earn them.

He sat in the wet chalk and laughed once, which hurt his chest, and then stopped.

Ferrous was nine miles.

[STATUS] wren — Level 2 | HP 13/22 | MP ?/? | Gold ?

The post five miles short of Ferrous had no name on the board, only **TALLOW** burnt into the upright a long time ago and painted over twice since.

There was a man sitting on the apron with his back against the post and his frame still on, which is a thing no porter does unless standing up again is the part he's saving strength for.

"You're the one with the wax," the man said.

Wren stopped. His left arm hung the way a rope hangs.

"Mekk." He didn't put out a hand. "Word came down from Hask before you did. Man took the through-carry and made it."

"Three days."

"Three days," Mekk agreed. He was maybe sixty, maybe less and used harder. "How much did they take off you in the dark to give it?"

Wren stood in the road with a crate on one shoulder and did not answer.

Mekk laughed without sound, which turned into a cough, which took a while. Then he went into his coat and brought out a thing folded to the softness of cloth — a sheet that had been paper once, worn white along the creases, the corners gone round like a stone in a stream. He opened it on his knee with two fingers, the way a man opens something he has opened ten thousand times.

Columns. Gate, load, toll, his own running number. And a fourth column, narrow, in a hand grown shakier down the years: *alone. queue. alone. warden. alone.*

At the top, in letters big enough to read at arm's length, one word. Not the same word Wren had used. Mekk's said **NOBODY WATCHING**.

"Eleven years," Mekk said. "Found it in my third. Everybody finds it in their third. You're quick, you found it in your fourth, that's not quick, that's just heavy." He smoothed the sheet flat. "Nine hundred and six days, that column's cost me. Give or take. My arithmetic's gone soft."

"You never said."

"I say it all the time. I said it to a boy at Rushet last spring. He said *thanks* and went and paid his toll." Mekk folded the sheet back along its own creases, one, two, three. "Everybody knows, porter. That's what I'm telling you and you're not hearing it. There's no secret. The query's two days. You pay your two days and the window tells you *the account is correct as recorded*, because it is — it's recorded, isn't it, so it's correct — and then you've paid two days to be told that, and now you're the man who paid two days to be told that, and nobody wants to be him twice."

"So nobody complains."

"So nobody complains." He put the sheet away. "We just walk slower and carry more and take a shift where there's a driver on the road, and call that being clever."

The collector came out then, an old woman with a lamp she didn't need in the daylight, and priced them both.

"Four, laden. Consent."

"I consent to the toll of four days against passage of the Tallow post, laden and sealed."

The stepping-back. Four of them, gone into some autumn.

The book on the sill: **Days owed: 3,999. Days paid: 101.** Three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine. Correct. The margin column, beside today, empty as a swept floor.

Because Mekk was standing there. Because there were two of them.

Then it was Mekk's turn, and he had to use the post to get up, and got up anyway, and came to the sill with his hands loose.

"Four, laden."

"I consent to the toll of four days against passage of the Tallow post, laden and sealed."

Wren was looking straight at him when the System took them.

There was no sound. There was no light. Mekk's face did the thing a face does when a man remembers something pleasant from a long way off, and his knee went, and the frame came down first because the frame always comes down first, and he folded over sideways onto the apron with his cheek in the swept chalk.

Wren was on his knees beside him before he knew he had gone down, hauling one-handed at the straps with his good arm, saying the man's name twice.

The collector set her lamp on the sill and looked at the book instead.

"He had three," she said.

"Three what."

"Three days. Remaining." She turned a page without hurry. "He consented to four."

"Then it shouldn't have gone through."

"Consent went through." She wrote. "The toll is the toll."

Wren stayed on the ground a while with his hand on a dead man's shoulder and his own shoulder screaming and the rattle going in and out of his chest.

Then he sat back on his heels and said, "You knew what he had left."

"I don't price what's left. I price the gate."

The route did not stop. That was the part he understood last. The consignment on Mekk's frame was for the Ferrous window and the tag said so, and a tag does not care, and the collector wrote *route reassigned to porter present* and asked Wren to consent aloud to the transfer, and Wren heard himself say the words.

He roped Mekk's crate high on his own, on the right, because the left was finished. Under the lid flap of Mekk's satchel there was an oilcloth roll, and inside it, chits. Grey ones, hundreds, punched and threaded on a cord by year, eleven years of a man's arithmetic against the Road's, every date, every gate, every number the book had ever written about him.

Wren put the roll inside his coat, against his ribs, where the rattle was.

Ferrous was five miles.

[STATUS] wren — Level 2 | HP 17/22 | MP ?/? | Gold ?

The depot behind the Ferrous window was a long shed with a hatch in its side, and Wren came at it out of the dark from the Tallow direction with two crates on his right shoulder and one arm hanging.

Up the line, at the gate itself, Haro's lamp was burning on the sill. Wren did not go that way.

The clerk at the hatch was a narrow man of about thirty with ink to the second knuckle. He read the tags without touching the crates.

"Ovenstone and Hask. That's the through-carry." He looked up. "You're the one."

"Route reassigned at Tallow. The other's Mekk's."

"Mekk's is Mekk's."

"Mekk's dead. Tallow post, this morning. The collector wrote *route reassigned to porter present*."

The clerk's pen stopped for the length of a breath, and then went on, which told Wren more about the road than the pause did.

"Then it's yours to sign in." He stamped, tore, passed a receipt across. "That's the two. The sealed one isn't mine."

"No."

"Then take it off my apron before you set it down." He said it without heat. "Anything else, porter, I'm past my hours."

"The old books."

"What about them."

"When a gate book fills. Where does it go."

The clerk put his pen in the trough and looked at Wren properly for the first time, at the arm, at the chalk still down one side of him from kneeling on the Tallow apron.

"Through there. Bound, shelved, dated." He tipped his head at a door behind him. "Closed books. Nobody reads them. There's a mouse in there I've named."

"I want an hour with them."

"That's a query. Query's two days, at the window, from Haro."

"The query gives me *the account is correct as recorded*. I want the record."

"Which is the same thing said slower." The clerk leaned on the hatch. "I can't take days off you. Days aren't mine. Only the System prices days and only at a gate, and I'm not a gate, I'm a man with a stamp."

"Then price it in something you can take."

There was a pause with the sea-sound of the shed's roof in it.

"Salt comes up from the barges at the ninth hour and wants moving to the depot floor. Two weeks of nights, unpaid, off the book — no entry, no chit, nothing anybody could ever ask me about."

"One week."

"You've got one arm."

"One week," Wren said, "and I start now."

The clerk looked at him a while.

"Half up front," he said. "Then your hour."

The sacks were four stone each and came off the barge lip onto a bare shoulder, and there was no strap and no frame, which meant carrying them the way a man carries a body. Wren took them on the right. Forty paces to the depot floor, stack, back. The tear across his thumb opened under the sacking twine on the ninth trip and he wrapped it and stopped counting after that. His breath had gone from a rattle to something with a whistle at the far end of it, and he found that if he went slower the whistle stayed smaller, so he went slower, and the clerk did not say anything about the pace, which was its own kind of decency.

At some hour with no name in it the clerk came out with a lamp and said, "That's the half."

The room behind the door was colder than the road. Books to the ceiling, spines dated in whitewash, and the smell of paper that has been damp once and dried badly.

The clerk set a glass on the shelf and turned it.

"One hour. You put every one back where it stood."

Wren went into his coat and brought out the oilcloth roll, and unthreaded the cord, and let eleven years of Mekk hang off his good hand in the lamplight. He took the oldest chit — punched, soft, the ink gone brown — and read the date and the gate off it, and pulled the book that matched.

Millrace. Eleven years back. A page ruled in the old way, four columns wide, the hand small and even.

He found Mekk on it. **Mekk — laden — 6 — days owed 8,904.** The chit in his fingers said six days, same date, same gate. It agreed. He had half expected it not to.

Then, eleven lines down the same page, past four other porters and a warden's crossing, he found six days again.

Same date. Same six. Not a toll — no name against it, no load, no consent noted. Just the figure, entered clean into a column the new books did not print, and beside it in the narrow margin a small letter and a numeral, set down in the same even hand.

He went back up the page. Beside Mekk's own line, in Mekk's own margin: the same letter, the same numeral.

The same days, written twice. Once as taken. Once as gone somewhere.

He turned pages with his thumb bleeding into the corner of them. Seven days out of a porter at Slate, and seven days again, unattached, further down. Five, and five. The margin letter paired every time, like a knot tied at both ends.

And on the older pages — the ones bound before somebody had decided the column was not worth printing — the column had a heading.
